Apokalupsis
ah-po-KAH-loop-sis
n. (Greek)
Greek apokalupsis, “an uncovering, revelation, disclosure,” from apokaluptō (to uncover, reveal), from apo- (off, from) + kaluptō (to cover, veil). The literal sense is off-veiling: the removing of a covering so that what was previously hidden is now seen.

📖 Biblical Definition

Apokalupsis is the New Testament’s great word for revelation—the divine uncovering of what would otherwise remain hidden. The word governs three major theological categories. First, the revelation of God in general: His self-disclosure in creation, in providence, in the prophetic word, and supremely in His Son. Romans 1:18 names the present revelation of God’s wrath against unrighteousness: for the wrath of God is revealed (apokaluptetai) from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. Romans 16:25-26 names the revelation of the mystery of the gospel, kept secret since the world began but now made manifest: according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith. Second, the revelation of God to specific recipients for the founding-and-shaping of the apostolic gospel. Paul received his gospel by the revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal 1:12); he writes of visions and revelations of the Lord (2 Cor 12:1); the apostles and prophets received the foundational revelations on which the church is built (Eph 2:20; 3:5). Third, and supremely climactic, the eschatological revelation: the parousia or apokalupsis of Christ at His second coming, the great unveiling at the end of the age. 1 Corinthians 1:7: waiting for the coming (apokalupsis) of our Lord Jesus Christ. 2 Thessalonians 1:7: when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed (apokalupsei) from heaven with his mighty angels. 1 Peter 1:7: that the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing (apokalupsei) of Jesus Christ. 1 Peter 1:13: hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation (apokalupsei) of Jesus Christ. The last book of the NT itself is named after this word: The Revelation (Apokalupsis) of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass (Rev 1:1). The book of Revelation is the climactic apokalupsis: the divine uncovering of what God will do at the end of the age, given to John on Patmos and through him to the churches of every age. The biblical doctrine of revelation is therefore structurally Trinitarian and Christological: God reveals; the Father gives the revelation to the Son; the Son gives it to His servants by His Spirit through His apostles and prophets; the church receives it in Scripture; the final and consummating revelation is the unveiling of Christ Himself at His coming, when every eye shall see Him and the saints shall be like Him.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 16:25-26 — "According to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith."

1 Peter 1:7 — "That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ."

Galatians 1:12 — "For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ."

Revelation 1:1 — "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Apokalupsis-shaped doctrine of revelation is corrupted, on one side, by the continuing-revelation traditions (charismatic, Roman Catholic, Mormon) that have placed extra-canonical sources on a level with the apostolic revelation closed in the New Testament—and on the other by the cessationist over-correction that has so feared continuing-revelation excesses that it has muted the Spirit’s present-age work of illumination and applied revelation through the closed canon.

expand to see more

The continuing-revelation corruption takes several forms across various traditions. Roman Catholicism has historically placed church tradition on a level with Scripture as the source of divine revelation. Mormonism has added the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants, and the Pearl of Great Price as continuing revelations. Charismatic and Pentecostal movements often function with prophecies and personal revelations that, while formally distinguished from Scripture, in practice exercise authority comparable to it. The Protestant doctrine of sola Scriptura insists that the foundational and authoritative revelation of God for the post-apostolic church is the closed canon of Scripture; the apostolic revelation, with the apostles having no successors in their unique founding office, is complete; subsequent claims of revelation are to be tested against Scripture and never to be placed on a level with it. The recovery is the recovery of the closed canon as the rule of faith and life, the sole infallible standard, the foundation upon which the church is built.

The opposite corruption is the cessationist over-correction that has so feared continuing-revelation excesses that it has muted the Spirit’s present-age work of illumination and applied revelation through the closed canon. The doctrine that the foundational revelation is closed (the canon is complete; no new Scripture-level revelations are being given; the apostles have no successors in their unique office) does not require the conclusion that the Spirit no longer illumines, applies, guides, convicts, or speaks through the closed canon to particular saints in particular providences. The historic Reformed tradition has consistently distinguished between foundational revelation (closed) and the Spirit’s ongoing application of the foundational revelation to His people in their particular situations (continuing). The Westminster Confession (1.6): the whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man’s salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men. Nevertheless, we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word. Both ends are required: closed canon as the foundational revelation, and ongoing Spirit-mediated illumination and application as the present-age work the same Spirit performs through the Word He inspired. Recover both, and the doctrine of revelation stands biblically and pastorally where it should: foundational and complete, but presently applied by the Spirit who is no less active for the canon’s closure.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apokalupsis (revelation, uncovering, disclosure), from apokaluptō (to uncover) from apo- + kaluptō (off-veiling)—the divine unveiling structurally Trinitarian and Christological, present in the apostolic foundation, ongoing in the Spirit’s illumination of the closed canon, and consummated in the eschatological apokalupsis of Christ at His second coming.

expand to see more

Greek apokalupsis (G602) — revelation, uncovering, disclosure (18 NT uses).

Greek apokaluptō (G601) — to uncover, reveal (26 NT uses).

Greek kaluptō (G2572) — to cover, veil (the cousin verb; the covering which the revelation uncovers).

Greek phaneroō (G5319) — to make manifest (the cousin revelation-verb of the NT).
